title: Fitting, then shrinking
sub: Least squares by gradient descent, and what ridge and lasso penalties do to the coefficients.

frames.caption: Fourteen noisy points. Start with the flat line y = 0. The red segments are the residuals; least squares minimizes the sum of their squares.
Gradient descent nudges the intercept and slope downhill on that sum. The residuals shrink quickly.
Closer. Note the residuals are measured vertically, in y only: x is assumed to be known exactly.

Converged to the same line the normal equations give in one shot: y = 2.12 + 0.68 x (the data were made with 1.5 + 0.8x plus noise). At the optimum the residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with x: they are orthogonal to the columns of X, which is the projection picture.

Six standardized features; only features 1 and 2 truly matter, and feature 4 is a decoy correlated with feature 1. Ridge regression: as the penalty λ grows (to the right), every coefficient shrinks towards zero.
But none of them reaches zero: the squared penalty gets weaker as a coefficient gets small, so ridge shrinks everything and selects nothing.
Lasso, the same data. The absolute-value penalty pushes with the same force no matter how small a coefficient is.
So irrelevant coefficients hit exactly zero and stay there: lasso performs feature selection as it shrinks.
With a large enough λ every coefficient is zero. In between there is a range where only the two real features survive.
